# Cons and Vectors {#sec-cons}

"Random access" sounds like a hardware claim. In this language it is an
indexing claim. Both structures live on the heap, in the collector's node
pools. The C stack and the protection stack are real, and they are not
where your list is stored.

## A cons cell is three pointers

Lisp's *cons* is short for *construct*. A {{< glossary "cons cell" >}} is
one node:

| Field | Role in R |
| --- | --- |
| CAR | the head, the value |
| CDR | the rest of the chain |
| TAG | an optional name, a `SYMSXP`, or Nil |

A pairlist of length three is three heap nodes linked by `CDR`, and the
last CDR is `R_NilValue`. Reaching element *i* walks *i* links. That cost
is linear. Attributes are stored this way. Formals are stored this way.
The manual is explicit that a `LANGSXP`, the type of a call, is a pairlist
whose CAR is the function and whose CDR is the arguments, tags included
when the caller named them.

You can see it in any classed object's attribute dump. `names` and `class`
are tags on a `LISTSXP`. The values hanging off those tags are ordinary
vectors, often a `STRSXP` of length one whose single `CHARSXP` is in the
string cache and has a ridiculous reference count because the cache is
doing its job. The structure around them is still a linked list. R did not
modernize that path. It stopped asking analysts to live on it.

## A generic vector is an array of pointers

A `VECSXP` is one header plus a contiguous block of `SEXP` pointers.
Element *i* is `data[i]`. That is constant time. That is all
"random access" means here. It does not mean the pairlist is on the stack,
and it does not mean the vector is a C array of unboxed values. The
pointers in a list refer to other nodes, which have their own headers,
their own counts, their own possibility of being shared.

Atomic vectors are the unboxed case: an `INTSXP` really is a block of C
`int`s, a `REALSXP` a block of `double`s. A list is a block of pointers
*to* values. Sharing a list and sharing an element of the list are
different facts. That difference is why changing one column of a data
frame does not have to copy the other columns. The vector of column
pointers is the thing that gets duplicated. The untouched columns keep
their addresses. [Advanced R's chapter on names and
values](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/names-values.html) is the patient version
of this, with pictures.

## Demoted, not deleted

Early R was closer to Scheme. Implementing a GNU S pushed the pairlist
inward and the vector outward. Chambers' history in the R Journal article
is the long version of that turn: an interface to Fortran arrays, a
user language of expressions that return objects, and an implementation
that grew a second, vector-shaped world on top of a cons-shaped evaluator.

What remains of the cons world at the surface:

- `pairlist()` and `as.pairlist()`, which most code never needs
- the occasional pairlist that leaks out of a primitive and gets coerced
  to a list on the way past
- `formals()`, which returns a pairlist because that is what a closure's
  formals *are*
- attributes, which you manipulate with `attr` and `attributes` so you
  never have to walk the chain yourself
- every call you `quote`, which is a `LANGSXP` and therefore a cons chain
  you are encouraged to treat as data

"R did not abandon cons; it demoted them to implementation substrate" is
this split, said in one line. Analysts get vectors and generic vectors.
The evaluator keeps cons cells for the sentences of the language and for
the metadata hung on values. When a pairlist crosses into user code it is
often promoted, because the user-facing sequence type won.

The terminology is scar tissue. In Lisp a list *is* a chain of conses. In
R a list is a `VECSXP`, and the chain of conses is called a pairlist so
that the two can coexist in one manual. If that naming bothers you, it
should. It is the sound of two languages that refused to give up their
word for the same idea.

## What you can see without a microscope

```r
typeof(quote(f(x = 1)))   # "language"  -> LANGSXP
typeof(formals(mean))     # often "pairlist"
typeof(list(a = 1))       # "list"      -> VECSXP
typeof(attributes(factor(1)))  # "pairlist" or NULL, and the class attribute is real
```

`lobstr::ast()` prints a call as a tree because the call *is* a tree of
cons cells. `lobstr::ref()` on a list shows you the pointer array and then
the children. The two pictures are the two worlds. Once you can see which
world a given object is in, a surprising number of performance folktales
become ordinary data-structure facts: walking a pairlist in a tight loop
is a linked-list walk, growing a vector without the true-length trick is
copying an array, and `[[` on a list is an index, not a search.

The protection stack is the other "stack" worth a sentence, so it stops
haunting the word. R's C API requires callers to protect nodes they want
to survive a garbage collection. That protection is a pointer stack in the
runtime, described around the memory-allocator sections of the internals
manual. It is bookkeeping for the collector. It is not the place pairlists
live, and it is not an invitation to reason about user objects as
stack-allocated values. User-visible SEXPs are heap nodes. Full stop.
